question: Is it permissible to enter competitions with an entrance fee and a prize, or is that gambling?
answer:
So there's a competition, and you have to pay $10 to participate, and the winning prize is $1,000. The brother is saying, can I participate? Or, you know, it's very common: a corporation has a fancy car (not for sale, for a prize), and they say, "$20 coupon. $20, you get the coupon, and we're going to pull one, and whoever gets that will get the car." So you're paying some money, and the goal is to get something more back.

Now, scenario B, the car: everybody here knows this is what? Gambling. The question is about scenario A, and he is saying, why is scenario A not the same as scenario B? That's the question. Is it halal? If it is, why isn't this like gambling? You're paying the $10 entrance fee, and we want to win the first prize, which is $500, $1,000, or an Umrah trip; it's only a $10 fee, and the Umrah trip is two thousand dollars. Why isn't that a type of gambling?

So, very good question, and I don't even think the questioner realizes how complicated this question is. And I kid you not, I have in my library three specific monographs and PhD dissertations written about this. It's not an easy topic. Entire books are written about the fiqh differences, the fiqh rulings about participating in competitions. It's not a simple answer. You have, as is to be expected, a whole spectrum of opinion.

Everybody agrees that if you purchase a ticket that is valueless in order to gain something valuable, this is gambling. Everybody agrees; there is ijma' on this point. And Allah says in the Qur'an, Surah al-Ma'idah verse 91: O you who believe, alcohol and gambling are filth from Shaytan. And Allah says: Shaytan wants to cause enmity between you via gambling and via alcohol, and Shaytan wants you to not worship Allah, via gambling and via khamr. So will you not pay attention?

And Ibn 'Abbas said: in the days of Jahiliyyah, a man would have a bet with another man with something of his valuables, or his property, or even sometimes his family. And whoever won, they would hand the other, you know, the item that they had bet, or they had lost, right? Whoever won would be handed it over. So this is something Allah forbade.

And that is why, by unanimous consensus of all the madhahib, **any type of lottery system in which you pay money for something that has no value, to have the chance to gain something that has value, this is haram.** Now, this is the lottery ticket.

After this, there are the controversial areas. What if you don't buy anything and it's an open competition? Okay, an open competition: you're not paying any money, and it's just an open competition. For example, you go grocery shopping, and the grocery store has: whoever is the 1000th person who comes in today will win a hundred-dollar card. Did you spend any money? No, you're just walking in and going shopping. In this case it is not lottery, because you're not spending any money. This is a gift that they're doing to advertise their business, and they can give whatever gift they want. You are not spending any money. So if you're not spending money, it's not an issue.

What if you spend money for an item, but the item has a coupon in it? For example, when we were children, I would love to buy cereals that have the coupons, or, what do you call it, box tops, whatever, right? Or sometimes the can, right?

I remember once the question was asked to me in Canada. I was teaching a class, and their famous brand is Tim Hortons, which, by the way, for the record, is not coffee, but that's beside the point. All the Canadian people watching are going to be boycotting me after this, but that's just colored water; that's not coffee. But anyway, I love Canadians, but Tim Hortons is not coffee. So Tim Hortons had a very big deal going on, and I was asked this question in class. They had thousands of prizes: if you purchase the coffee, you unroll the cup: a million dollars, a car, a house. I mean, Tim Hortons is a multi-billion-dollar corporation; they were giving prizes after prizes, right? So, for some weird reason they like that brand, so everybody's drinking Tim Hortons, and a Muslim brother won something. A Muslim brother won something. So is this halal?

The response: this is a gray area. The majority of ulama of our time say (listen to this): if the goal and the intention was that you're purchasing the product for the product, and the product is being advertised at the same price (everybody knows it's the same coffee), and your niyyah, and Allah knows your niyyah, is that you want to drink the coffee, you want to get the cereal box, you want to do whatever, and this comes as a secondary thing, not the primary, then it is permissible. Because your goal was not to purchase the coffee for the rare chance of getting the million dollars; your goal was to get the coffee and drink it. Okay? So in this case the niyyah does count.

And our shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin also said that the corporation should not increase the price to demonstrate that there's an extra fee: "If you want to participate, you pay more." It should be the same price. So the coffee is $1.50, and then they advertise, "Okay, anybody who buys has a chance in a million to get a million dollars"; the coffee should still be $1.50. You should not have "if you want to participate, then you have to pay for the $2 coffee." You get the point. It should be the same price, and the niyyah should be, "I want to purchase for the sake of that." In this case, because this is an incentive that people should be buying, it's not lottery per se. There is a position that says it is lottery, and that's fine, but the majority of scholars of our time say this would not be considered to be a lottery.

The third and final scenario, which is what he is asking: what if it's not pure luck but some skill? That's what he is saying: competition. What if it's a competition? And this is really the meat of the matter. This is where the controversy occurs amongst the classical fuqaha. I'm going to summarize. Believe it or not, it's not that simple.

Why? Because of the hadith in Abu Dawud: our Prophet ﷺ said, "There should be no competition except in arrows and horses and camels." I'm paraphrasing: la sabaqa illa fi nasl aw khuff aw hafir. It is authentic, in Abu Dawud. Now, what does "there should be no competition" mean? Everybody understands this means there should be no money for competition. Obviously I can have a competition for anything: who has the cleanest house. Here, what is being talked about is gambling money, you know, the horse gambling and what not. There should be no competition for money except in these three things. Now, what does this mean? If there is to be money, then it is allowed to have monetary competitions for arrows, for horses, and for camels.

Can anybody guess why these three are allowed? Firstly, before we get to exceptions: because all three are, let's just say, defense mechanisms. Let's just say this is a legitimate struggle, and there are times when one needs to struggle to protect one's family and honor. And so these three things are defense mechanisms. Okay?

So because of this, the Shari'ah has allowed it: go ahead and encourage the people. Let them aim better, right? Let them train their horses. We want to encourage this. Why? Because when there's a thousand-dollar prize for whoever has the fastest horse, what's going to happen? A hundred people will train their horses. Okay? And even if one wins the prize, the other 99, if there is ever a struggle, can struggle along with those who struggle. Okay? So the ummah benefits. Therefore our Prophet ﷺ is saying: if there must be a competition, do it for these types of things.

Now, does this mean that everybody can then pay $100 and one person wins the $1,000 prize, or $10 and the $1,000? This is where the controversy occurs.

The majority opinion is as follows: if the money comes from a third party, then everything is legit and halal. The ruler says a thousand dollars, or a corporation says, "These are for the top one, two, three," and it is free of charge for the people: no problem. This is the majority opinion for any competition: no problem, because you're not the one paying, as we said. So if a third party gives the money, no problem, whatever the competition.

But the majority interpret this hadith: if you're going to pay an amount, then the only scenario in which this is allowed is these three. Do you understand? And by the way, whatever I'm saying, there are always other opinions; I'm just giving you the default so that we understand the concept.

This is a position. This is Ibn Taymiyyah's position, it is the position of the Hanafi school and others, other madhhabs as well: that if you're going to pay fees and participate, it had better be for defense mechanisms, for something that is mutually beneficial for the ummah, and not something that is not mutually beneficial. In that case, only if the money is from a third party is it halal; you cannot pay money to participate in that. Do you understand this? Okay.

The other madhhabs said: if you are paying your money, it is only halal if some people are also participating who are not paying money, in which case it's not gambling. Where do they get this from? The hadith in Abu Dawud: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever adds another horse to the two horses that are racing, and there is no guarantee that that horse might win or lose..." I.e., two people have put the money: two people have put $100, $100, and they say whoever wins will get the $200. Is that clear? Right? The Prophet ﷺ said: if a third horse comes in without any money, and the horse is of similar speed as the others (you don't bring an old horse, you don't bring a lame horse, you don't bring a blind horse; similar), then in that case it is not gambling, even if they put their own money, and then another person comes in.

So what this means... The safer opinion is as follows, and this is the majority opinion: Islamic competitions have the same ruling as these three, because they benefit the ummah. Whoever memorizes the Qur'an first, whoever answers all of these questions of the Hadith Nawawi quiz first, whoever does the fiqh exam and scores the highest grade.

Now, guys, understand me: if the money comes from the masjid, haram or halal? 100% halal. If the money comes from a third party, 100% halal. We are talking about if the students have to pay money; this is the whole scenario of potential gambling.

The majority opinion is as follows: it is not allowed to hold such a competition where everybody pays 10 dollars and from that money the first prize is a thousand, the second prize is five hundred, unless you bring in one or two or three other students who are equally qualified and who what? Who don't pay any fees. Okay? This is the majority opinion.

Now, Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and even the Hanafi madhhab disagreed, and they said no. This other hadith they interpreted in a bit of a complicated structure, which we're not going to go into. And they basically said: no, it is allowed, when there is maslahah for the ummah, for everybody to be equally participating with money, because the goal is to incentivize the ummah. And they used the first hadith, which is "there is no competition except in these three," and they said the whole point of the competition is what? To bring in money. And some of them considered the other hadith to be weak, and others said it is abrogated, and others brought their interpretation.

The bottom line, and with this we conclude, inshallah: **inshallah it is permissible to have an Islamic competition that benefits the ummah, in any area that the ummah collectively benefits from, where students or participants put in a fee, and that fee is used for the grand prize.**

However, to get out of the khilaf (Ibn Taymiyyah said it's halal, as did Ibn al-Qayyim), it would always be wise to bring in one or two students who don't pay anything. And maybe a lottery system: everybody pays, then one person, you just pull out and say, "Okay, you get a free one." Maybe this way, so that you follow the safer opinion and say, okay, now this is not lottery or gambling, because there are some people, or even one person, but as long as they're all equally coming in. You haven't hedged the bets yourself; you haven't yourself structured it so that, okay, the weakest student doesn't pay. No, not like that. Everybody should come equally, then one or two should not pay. Then it is out of the khilaf, and all the madhhabs would allow it.

Nonetheless, if the structure is not like that, then Ibn al-Qayyim has a long passage in his book Kitab al-Furusiyyah, which is a book about these types of things, horse rearing or what not, and he says it's completely halal. You're allowed to do this, because it benefits the ummah, and because of the hadith. And Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.

As for the youth and basketball tournaments, I would also say at least one should not pay. This is my opinion: at least one should not pay, so that it then becomes permissible. And Allah knows best.
